questions.stem: An index number is best described as:

options.text: The arithmetic average of a set of prices in the current year
options.explanation: An average of prices carries a unit and is distorted by the units chosen. An index number is a pure ratio measured against a base.

options.text: A number that measures the relative change in a variable or a group of variables between a current period and a base period, the base being set at 100
options.explanation: Correct. An index number expresses the current situation as a percentage of a base situation fixed at 100, so it measures net relative change without carrying any unit.

options.text: The total money value of all goods traded in the current year
options.explanation: That is aggregate value, not an index. An index compares two periods and is a pure number.

options.text: The difference between the current price and the base price of a commodity
options.explanation: A difference is an absolute change in one price. An index number is a ratio, and it summarises a group, not a single commodity.

readLink.label: Read: What an index number is, §1 →

questions.stem: In an index number series the base period value is:

options.text: Always the largest value in the series
options.explanation: The base is chosen as a normal period, not a peak. It need not be the largest value.

options.text: Set equal to the current period value
options.explanation: The base and current periods are different periods; the base is the reference against which the current period is compared.

options.text: Always set equal to 100, so every other figure is read as a percentage of it
options.explanation: Correct. The base period is fixed at 100 by convention, so an index of 130 means a 30% rise over the base and 92 means an 8% fall.

options.text: Set equal to zero at the start of the series
options.explanation: An index measures a ratio, not a difference, so the base is 100 rather than 0.

readLink.label: Read: What an index number is, §1 →

questions.stem: A commodity cost ₹ 25 in the base year and ₹ 30 in the current year. Its price relative is:

options.explanation: Correct. Price relative = p₁ ÷ p₀ × 100 = 30 ÷ 25 × 100 = 120, a 20% rise over the base year.
This is the reverse ratio, 25 ÷ 30 × 100. The current price goes on top of the base price, not below it.
This is the percentage rise, (30 − 25) ÷ 25 × 100. The relative is the whole ratio, 120, not just the increase.
This adds the ₹ 5 rise to 100. A price relative is a ratio times 100, not the base plus the rupee change.

questions.stem: The price of a commodity rose from ₹ 80 in the base year to ₹ 100 in the current year. The price relative is:

options.explanation: This is the reverse ratio, 80 ÷ 100 × 100. Current price divided by base price gives the relative.
This is the percentage rise, (100 − 80) ÷ 80 × 100. The relative is the full ratio, not the increase alone.
This is the rupee change ₹ 20, not a relative. A relative is a ratio expressed as a percentage.
Correct. Price relative = 100 ÷ 80 × 100 = 125, a 25% rise over the base year.

questions.stem: Four commodities had base-year prices ₹ 25, ₹ 20, ₹ 15 and ₹ 40, and current-year prices ₹ 30, ₹ 24, ₹ 20 and ₹ 46. The simple aggregate price index is:

options.explanation: This is the simple average of the four price relatives, a different method. The simple aggregate divides the sum of current prices by the sum of base prices.
This is the reverse ratio, Σp₀ ÷ Σp₁ × 100. Current prices go on top.
This does not match either sum. Add the four current prices (120) and the four base prices (100) and divide.

questions.topic: Ch 18 · Simple average of price relatives
questions.stem: For four commodities the prices moved 40 → 50, 20 → 25, 50 → 60 and 25 → 30 (base → current). The simple average of price relatives is:

options.explanation: This is the simple aggregate, Σp₁ ÷ Σp₀ × 100 = 165 ÷ 135 × 100. The simple average of relatives averages the four relatives instead.
This is the sum of the four relatives (125 + 125 + 120 + 120) without dividing by N = 4.
Correct. The relatives are 125, 125, 120 and 120, and their average is 490 ÷ 4 = 122.5.
This is only two of the four relatives. All four must be averaged: (125 + 125 + 120 + 120) ÷ 4.

readLink.label: Read: Simple average of price relatives, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Simple average of relatives = Σ(p₁ ÷ p₀ × 100) ÷ N

questions.stem: The chief defect of the simple aggregate price index is that:

options.text: It is distorted by the units in which prices are quoted, and gives every commodity equal importance
options.explanation: Correct. A price quoted per quintal swamps one quoted per kilogram, and each commodity counts alike regardless of how much is bought. Relatives cure the first fault and weighting the second.

options.text: It cannot be computed when prices rise
options.explanation: It can be computed for any prices; the objection is that the result is unreliable, not that it fails to exist.

options.text: It always understates the true change in prices
options.explanation: It can read too high or too low depending on the units chosen; the bias has no fixed direction.

options.text: It requires current-year quantity data that are hard to collect
options.explanation: The simple aggregate uses no quantities at all. That objection applies to the Paasche index.

questions.sourceRef: Limitations of the simple aggregate index

questions.stem: Three commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (6, 10, 10, 12); B (2, 20, 3, 25); C (4, 15, 5, 10). The Laspeyres price index is:

options.explanation: This is the Paasche index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100. Laspeyres uses base-year quantities q₀, not current quantities.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100, which mixes price and quantity change. Laspeyres weights current prices by base quantities.
Correct. Laspeyres = Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 = 235 ÷ 160 × 100 = 146.88, using Σp₁q₀ = 100 + 60 + 75 and Σp₀q₀ = 60 + 40 + 60.
This is Fisher's index, the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche. It is not Laspeyres itself.

questions.stem: For the same three commodities — A (6, 10, 10, 12); B (2, 20, 3, 25); C (4, 15, 5, 10) as (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁) — the Paasche price index is:

options.explanation: Correct. Paasche = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100 = 245 ÷ 162 × 100 = 151.23, using Σp₁q₁ = 120 + 75 + 50 and Σp₀q₁ = 72 + 50 + 40.
This is the Laspeyres index, which weights by base-year quantities q₀. Paasche weights by current-year quantities q₁.
This is Fisher's index, the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche, not Paasche alone.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Paasche keeps current quantities in both numerator and denominator.

questions.stem: Four commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (5, 50, 8, 60); B (8, 40, 10, 30); C (12, 20, 15, 25); D (4, 100, 5, 90). Fisher's ideal price index is:

options.explanation: This is the Paasche index alone. Fisher is the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche, so it lies below the higher of the two.
Correct. Laspeyres = 1600 ÷ 1210 × 100 = 132.23 and Paasche = 1605 ÷ 1200 × 100 = 133.75, so Fisher = square root of (132.23 × 133.75) = 132.99.
This is the Laspeyres index alone. Fisher lies between Laspeyres and Paasche, above this figure.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Fisher is built from Laspeyres and Paasche, not from the value ratio.

questions.stem: For the four commodities A (5, 50, 8, 60); B (8, 40, 10, 30); C (12, 20, 15, 25); D (4, 100, 5, 90) as (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁), the Laspeyres price index is:

options.explanation: This is the Paasche index, weighted by current quantities q₁. Laspeyres uses base quantities q₀.
This is Fisher's index, the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche, not Laspeyres itself.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Laspeyres holds base quantities in both sums.
Correct. Laspeyres = Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 = 1600 ÷ 1210 × 100 = 132.23.

questions.stem: For the four commodities A (5, 50, 8, 60); B (8, 40, 10, 30); C (12, 20, 15, 25); D (4, 100, 5, 90) as (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁), the Paasche price index is:

options.explanation: Correct. Paasche = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100 = 1605 ÷ 1200 × 100 = 133.75, using current-year quantities as weights.
This is the Laspeyres index, weighted by base quantities q₀. Paasche uses current quantities q₁.
This is Fisher's index, the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche, not Paasche alone.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Paasche keeps current quantities in both numerator and denominator.

questions.stem: Three commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (10, 12, 12, 15); B (8, 15, 10, 10); C (6, 24, 8, 20). The Marshall-Edgeworth price index is:

options.explanation: This is the Laspeyres index, Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 = 486 ÷ 384 × 100. Marshall-Edgeworth uses (q₀ + q₁) as the weight.
This is the Paasche index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100 = 440 ÷ 350 × 100. Marshall-Edgeworth combines both weights.
Correct. Marshall-Edgeworth = (Σp₁q₀ + Σp₁q₁) ÷ (Σp₀q₀ + Σp₀q₁) × 100 = (486 + 440) ÷ (384 + 350) × 100 = 926 ÷ 734 × 100 = 126.16.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 = 440 ÷ 384 × 100. It mixes price and quantity change.

questions.stem: For three commodities A (6, 10, 10, 12); B (2, 20, 3, 25); C (4, 15, 5, 10) as (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁), the Dorbish-Bowley price index is:

options.explanation: This is the Laspeyres index alone. Dorbish-Bowley is the arithmetic mean of Laspeyres and Paasche.
This is the Paasche index alone. Dorbish-Bowley averages Laspeyres and Paasche.
This is the sum of Laspeyres and Paasche without dividing by 2. Dorbish-Bowley is their mean.

questions.stem: Fisher's ideal index is the:

options.text: Arithmetic mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices
options.explanation: The arithmetic mean of the two is the Dorbish-Bowley index. Fisher uses the geometric mean.

options.text: Sum of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices
options.explanation: Fisher is a mean, not a sum. It lies between the two, not above both.

options.text: Larger of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices
options.explanation: Fisher lies between the two indices, so it is never the larger of them.

options.text: Geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche indices — the square root of their product
options.explanation: Correct. Fisher = square root of (Laspeyres × Paasche), which sits between the two and passes both reversal tests.

questions.sourceRef: Fisher is the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche

questions.stem: Three commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (10, 12, 12, 15); B (8, 15, 10, 10); C (6, 24, 8, 20). The Laspeyres price index is:

options.explanation: Correct. Laspeyres = Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 = 486 ÷ 384 × 100 = 126.56, using Σp₁q₀ = 144 + 150 + 192 and Σp₀q₀ = 120 + 120 + 144.
This is the Paasche index, weighted by current quantities q₁. Laspeyres uses base quantities q₀.
This is Fisher's index, the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche, not Laspeyres itself.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Laspeyres holds base quantities in both sums.

questions.stem: For the three commodities A (10, 12, 12, 15); B (8, 15, 10, 10); C (6, 24, 8, 20) as (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁), the Paasche price index is:

options.explanation: This is the Laspeyres index, weighted by base quantities q₀. Paasche uses current quantities q₁.
This is Fisher's index, the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche, not Paasche alone.
Correct. Paasche = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100 = 440 ÷ 350 × 100 = 125.71, using Σp₁q₁ = 180 + 100 + 160 and Σp₀q₁ = 150 + 80 + 120.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Paasche keeps current quantities in both sums.

questions.stem: Three commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (6, 10, 10, 12); B (2, 20, 3, 25); C (4, 15, 5, 10). Fisher's ideal price index is:

options.explanation: This is the Laspeyres index alone. Fisher is the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche.
Correct. Laspeyres = 235 ÷ 160 × 100 = 146.88 and Paasche = 245 ÷ 162 × 100 = 151.23, so Fisher = square root of (146.88 × 151.23) = 149.04.
This is the Paasche index alone. Fisher lies below the higher of the two indices.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Fisher is built from Laspeyres and Paasche.

questions.stem: Fisher's index is called the ideal index number mainly because it:

options.text: Satisfies both the time-reversal test and the factor-reversal test
options.explanation: Correct. Alone among the standard weighted indices, Fisher passes both reversal tests, and it also balances the upward Laspeyres bias against the downward Paasche bias.

options.text: Is the easiest of all the index numbers to compute
options.explanation: Fisher needs both Laspeyres and Paasche and then a square root, so it is more work, not less. Ease is not why it is ideal.

options.text: Uses only base-year quantities as weights
options.explanation: That describes Laspeyres. Fisher uses both base and current weights through the two indices it combines.

options.text: Always equals 100 in every period
options.explanation: No index stays at 100 once prices move. Fisher varies with prices like any other index.

readLink.label: Read: The tests of a good index number, §10 →

questions.stem: For the data A (5, 50, 8, 60); B (8, 40, 10, 30); C (12, 20, 15, 25); D (4, 100, 5, 90) as (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁), the product P₀₁ × P₁₀ using Fisher's index (both taken as ratios) equals:

options.explanation: The product of two positive index ratios cannot be zero. The time-reversal test requires it to equal 1.
This keeps the ×100 in each index. Used as ratios, Fisher's P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1, not 100.
Correct. Fisher's index satisfies the time-reversal test: P₀₁ (1.3299) × P₁₀ (0.7519) = 1, so reversing the periods reverses the index exactly.
This is Fisher's index P₀₁ itself. The test multiplies it by the reversed index P₁₀, giving 1.

readLink.label: Read: The tests of a good index number, §10 →

questions.sourceRef: Time-reversal test: P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1 for Fisher

questions.stem: For the data A (6, 10, 10, 12); B (2, 20, 3, 25); C (4, 15, 5, 10) as (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁), Fisher's price index times Fisher's quantity index (both as ratios) equals the value ratio Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀, which is:

options.explanation: That is the result of the time-reversal test, not the factor-reversal test. The factor-reversal test gives the value ratio.
Correct. The value ratio = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ = 245 ÷ 160 = 1.5313, and Fisher's price ratio times Fisher's quantity ratio reproduces it exactly, which is the factor-reversal test.
This is Fisher's price index as a ratio (149.04 ÷ 100). The factor-reversal test multiplies it by the Fisher quantity ratio to reach the value ratio.
This is the value index expressed as a percentage. As a ratio, for use in the test, it is 1.5313.

readLink.label: Read: The tests of a good index number, §10 →

questions.sourceRef: Factor-reversal test: P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ for Fisher

questions.stem: The time-reversal test is satisfied when (indices taken as ratios):

options.text: P₀₁ + P₁₀ = 1
options.explanation: The test multiplies the two indices, it does not add them. The sum of two ratios near 1.3 and 0.75 is about 2, not 1.

options.text: P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = value ratio
options.explanation: That is the factor-reversal test, which pairs a price index with a quantity index. The time-reversal test pairs the price index with its own reverse.

options.text: P₀₁ = P₁₀
options.explanation: The forward and reverse indices are reciprocals, not equals. Their product, not their equality, is the test.

options.text: P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1
options.explanation: Correct. Reversing the periods should invert the index, so the forward and reverse ratios multiply to 1. Fisher satisfies this; Laspeyres and Paasche do not.

readLink.label: Read: The tests of a good index number, §10 →

questions.stem: The factor-reversal test is satisfied when (indices taken as ratios):

options.text: P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀
options.explanation: Correct. The price index times the quantity index should equal the value ratio, because price times quantity is value. Fisher satisfies this; Laspeyres and Paasche do not.

options.text: P₀₁ × P₁₀ = 1
options.explanation: That is the time-reversal test, which pairs the price index with its own reverse. The factor-reversal test pairs price with quantity.

options.text: P₀₁ + Q₀₁ = 1
options.explanation: The test multiplies the price and quantity indices; it does not add them, and the result is the value ratio, not 1.

options.text: P₀₁ = Q₀₁
options.explanation: Price and quantity indices are generally different. Their product equalling the value ratio is the test, not their equality.

readLink.label: Read: The tests of a good index number, §10 →

questions.sourceRef: Factor-reversal test: P₀₁ × Q₀₁ = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀

questions.stem: Four commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (5, 50, 8, 60); B (8, 40, 10, 30); C (12, 20, 15, 25); D (4, 100, 5, 90). The Laspeyres quantity index is:

options.explanation: This is the reverse ratio, Σq₀p₀ ÷ Σq₁p₀ × 100. The current quantities go on top in a quantity index.
This is the Laspeyres price index. A quantity index weights quantities by prices, using Σq₁p₀ over Σq₀p₀.
Correct. Laspeyres quantity index = Σq₁p₀ ÷ Σq₀p₀ × 100 = Σp₀q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 = 1200 ÷ 1210 × 100 = 99.17, so quantities barely moved.
This is the Fisher quantity index, the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche quantity indices, not the Laspeyres quantity index alone.

readLink.label: Read: Quantity and value index numbers, §11 →

questions.stem: For the four commodities A (5, 50, 8, 60); B (8, 40, 10, 30); C (12, 20, 15, 25); D (4, 100, 5, 90) as (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁), the value index is:

options.explanation: This is the Laspeyres price index, Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. The value index uses current values in the numerator, Σp₁q₁.
This is the Paasche price index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100. The value index divides by base-year value, Σp₀q₀.
This is Fisher's price index. The value index is a separate quantity, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100.
Correct. Value index = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 = 1605 ÷ 1210 × 100 = 132.64, which combines both price and quantity change.

readLink.label: Read: Quantity and value index numbers, §11 →

questions.topic: Ch 18 · Cost of living · Aggregate expenditure
questions.stem: A family's basket has (p₀, q₀, p₁): item 1 (8, 25, 10); item 2 (6, 50, 7); item 3 (5, 20, 6). The cost of living index by the aggregate expenditure method is:

options.explanation: This is the simple average of the three price relatives (125, 116.67, 120), which ignores the quantities. The aggregate expenditure method weights by base quantities.
This is the reverse ratio, Σp₀q₀ ÷ Σp₁q₀ × 100. Current-year expenditure on the base basket goes on top.
This matches neither sum. Compute Σp₁q₀ = 720 and Σp₀q₀ = 600 and divide.

questions.topic: Ch 18 · Cost of living · Family budget
questions.stem: A consumer price index has five groups with (group index R, weight W): Food (140, 50); Clothing (120, 10); Fuel and light (110, 15); Rent (125, 15); Miscellaneous (130, 10). By the family budget method the index is:

options.explanation: This is Σ(RW) before dividing by ΣW. The weights total 100, so divide the 13,025 by 100.
This is the unweighted mean of the five group indices, (140 + 120 + 110 + 125 + 130) ÷ 5. The family budget method weights each index by W.
An index of 100 would mean no change. The RW total of 13,025 over a weight of 100 gives 130.25.

questions.sourceRef: Cost of living (family budget) = Σ(RW) ÷ ΣW

questions.stem: The cost of living index number (consumer price index) measures:

options.text: The change in the wholesale price of a single commodity
options.explanation: That is a price relative for one commodity at wholesale. The cost of living index covers a whole retail basket for a defined group.

options.text: The change in industrial output over a year
options.explanation: That is the index of industrial production, a quantity index. The cost of living index tracks prices of a consumption basket.

options.text: The change in the cost of a fixed basket of goods and services bought by a defined group of consumers
options.explanation: Correct. It tracks how much a fixed basket, representative of a particular group, costs over time, and is used to revise wages and dearness allowance.

options.text: The change in the exchange rate of the rupee
options.explanation: The exchange rate is a different measure. The cost of living index compares the cost of a consumption basket across periods.

questions.sourceRef: Cost of living index measures the cost of a fixed basket

questions.stem: A worker earns ₹ 18,000 a month when the cost of living index stands at 120 (base year = 100). The real wage, in base-year rupees, is:

options.explanation: This multiplies the money wage by 120 ÷ 100 instead of dividing. Deflating divides by the index and restores the base of 100.
This leaves the money wage unchanged, ignoring the 20% rise in prices. The real wage must be lower than the money wage when the index exceeds 100.
This deflates by 125 rather than the given index of 120. Use the index stated in the question.
Correct. Real wage = money wage ÷ index × 100 = 18,000 ÷ 120 × 100 = ₹ 15,000, the base-year purchasing power of the current pay.

questions.sourceRef: Real wage = (money wage ÷ cost of living index) × 100

questions.topic: Ch 18 · Purchasing power of the rupee
questions.stem: When the cost of living index is 125 (base year = 100), the purchasing power of the rupee, in base-year rupees, is:

options.explanation: Correct. Purchasing power = 100 ÷ index = 100 ÷ 125 = ₹ 0.80, so a rupee now buys 80 paise of what it bought in the base year.
This is index ÷ 100. The purchasing power is the reciprocal, 100 ÷ index, and must be below ₹ 1 once prices have risen.
This subtracts 0.25 from 1. The purchasing power is 100 ÷ 125 = 0.80, not 1 minus the fractional rise.
The rupee holds its full value only when the index is 100. At 125 its purchasing power has fallen to ₹ 0.80.

questions.sourceRef: Purchasing power of the rupee = 100 ÷ cost of living index

questions.stem: An employee is paid ₹ 24,000 a month when the cost of living index is 150 (base year = 100). The real wage, in base-year rupees, is:

options.explanation: This multiplies by 150 ÷ 100 instead of dividing. Deflating always divides the money wage by the index.
This leaves the money wage unchanged. With the index at 150, prices are half as high again, so the real wage is well below the money wage.
Correct. Real wage = 24,000 ÷ 150 × 100 = ₹ 16,000, the base-year value of the current pay.
This deflates by 160 rather than 150. Use the index given, 150, so the answer is ₹ 16,000.

questions.sourceRef: Real wage = (money wage ÷ cost of living index) × 100

questions.stem: Deflating a money wage means:

options.text: Increasing the money wage by the rate of inflation
options.explanation: That would raise the money figure, not remove the price effect. Deflating strips the price rise out to reveal real value.

options.text: Dividing the money wage by the cost of living index and restoring the base of 100, to find its real value
options.explanation: Correct. Deflating removes the price effect: real wage = money wage ÷ index × 100, giving the base-year purchasing power of the pay.

options.text: Multiplying the money wage by the cost of living index
options.explanation: Multiplying by the index inflates the figure further. Deflating divides by it.

options.text: Subtracting the base wage from the current wage
options.explanation: That is an absolute money difference, not a real value. Deflating uses the index, not a subtraction.

questions.sourceRef: Deflating removes the price effect from a money figure

questions.stem: A price index series reads 2019 = 100, 2020 = 120, 2021 = 150, 2022 = 180. If the base is shifted to 2021 = 100, the index for 2022 becomes:

options.explanation: This subtracts 30 from 180. Base shifting divides by the new base year's old index, 150, and multiplies by 100.
This is the reverse ratio, 150 ÷ 180 × 100. The current year's index goes on top.
This is the rupee-style difference 180 − 150, not a rebased index. Divide 180 by 150 and multiply by 100.
Correct. New index = old index of 2022 ÷ old index of 2021 × 100 = 180 ÷ 150 × 100 = 120.

questions.sourceRef: Base shifting: new index = (old index of year ÷ old index of new base) × 100

questions.stem: An old index series ends at 2020 = 150. A new series begins 2020 = 100, 2021 = 110, 2022 = 125. Splicing the new series onto the old base, the 2022 figure is:

options.explanation: Correct. Spliced figure = new index × (old overlap value ÷ 100) = 125 × 150 ÷ 100 = 187.5, so the new series is rescaled to the old base.
This is the reverse ratio, 125 × 100 ÷ 150. To carry the new series onto the old base, multiply by 150 ÷ 100.
This adds 125 and 150. Splicing multiplies the new figure by the overlap ratio, it does not add the two.
This is the unspliced new-series figure. Splicing rescales it by the overlap ratio 150 ÷ 100 = 1.5.

questions.stem: Base shifting is used to:

options.text: Collect fresh prices for a new base year
options.explanation: Base shifting needs no new data; it works entirely from the existing index series. Fresh prices would be a full re-basing exercise, not base shifting.

options.text: Join two overlapping index series into one continuous series
options.explanation: That is splicing. Base shifting re-expresses a single series on a new base, it does not join two series.

options.text: Re-express an existing index series on a new, more recent base year without collecting new data
options.explanation: Correct. Divide every figure by the old index of the chosen new base year and multiply by 100; the series is unchanged in shape, only the year reading 100 moves.

options.text: Convert a price index into a quantity index
options.explanation: Base shifting keeps the same variable; it only changes the reference year. Price and quantity indices are computed from different formulas.

questions.stem: Splicing of index numbers is the technique of:

options.text: Removing the price effect from a money figure
options.explanation: That is deflating. Splicing joins two index series, it does not convert money to real value.

options.text: Averaging the Laspeyres and Paasche indices
options.explanation: Averaging the two gives the Dorbish-Bowley index. Splicing links two series that overlap in a year.

options.text: Shifting a single series to a new base year
options.explanation: That is base shifting. Splicing works on two different series, not one.

options.text: Joining two overlapping index series, computed on different bases, into one continuous series
options.explanation: Correct. Using the overlap year, the new series is rescaled by the old series' value so the combined series runs on one scale with no jump.

questions.stem: Three commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (10, 12, 12, 15); B (8, 15, 10, 10); C (6, 24, 8, 20). Fisher's ideal price index is:

options.explanation: This is the Laspeyres index alone, 486 ÷ 384 × 100. Fisher is the geometric mean of Laspeyres and Paasche.
Correct. Laspeyres = 486 ÷ 384 × 100 = 126.56 and Paasche = 440 ÷ 350 × 100 = 125.71, so Fisher = square root of (126.56 × 125.71) = 126.14.
This is the Paasche index alone, 440 ÷ 350 × 100. Fisher lies between Laspeyres and Paasche.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Fisher is built from the Laspeyres and Paasche price indices.

questions.stem: Three commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (10, 12, 12, 15); B (8, 15, 10, 10); C (6, 24, 8, 20). The Laspeyres quantity index is:

options.explanation: Correct. Laspeyres quantity index = Σq₁p₀ ÷ Σq₀p₀ × 100 = Σp₀q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 = 350 ÷ 384 × 100 = 91.15, so quantities fell overall.
This is the Laspeyres price index. A quantity index weights the current quantities by base prices, using Σq₁p₀ over Σq₀p₀.
This is the reverse ratio, Σp₀q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100 = 384 ÷ 350 × 100. Current quantities go on top.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. A quantity index holds prices fixed as the weights.

readLink.label: Read: Quantity and value index numbers, §11 →

questions.stem: Three commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (6, 10, 10, 12); B (2, 20, 3, 25); C (4, 15, 5, 10). The value index is:

options.explanation: This is the Laspeyres price index, Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. The value index uses current values, Σp₁q₁, in the numerator.
This is the Paasche price index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100. The value index divides by base-year value, Σp₀q₀.
Correct. Value index = Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100 = 245 ÷ 160 × 100 = 153.13, combining both price and quantity change.
This is Fisher's price index. The value index is the ratio of total current value to total base value.

readLink.label: Read: Quantity and value index numbers, §11 →

questions.stem: A supervisor earns ₹ 30,000 a month when the cost of living index is 125 (base year = 100). The real wage, in base-year rupees, is:

options.explanation: This multiplies by 125 ÷ 100. Deflating divides the money wage by the index and multiplies by 100.
This leaves the money wage unchanged, ignoring the 25% rise in prices. The real wage must be lower.
This deflates by 120 rather than 125. Use the index stated, 125, giving ₹ 24,000.
Correct. Real wage = 30,000 ÷ 125 × 100 = ₹ 24,000, the base-year value of the current pay.

questions.sourceRef: Real wage = (money wage ÷ cost of living index) × 100

questions.topic: Ch 18 · Purchasing power of the rupee
questions.stem: When the cost of living index is 250 (base year = 100), the purchasing power of the rupee, in base-year rupees, is:

options.explanation: Correct. Purchasing power = 100 ÷ index = 100 ÷ 250 = ₹ 0.40, so a rupee now buys 40 paise of what it once did.
This is index ÷ 100. The purchasing power is the reciprocal, 100 ÷ index, and falls as prices rise.
This divides by 400, not 250. The purchasing power is 100 ÷ 250 = ₹ 0.40.
This subtracts 0.40 from 1. The purchasing power is 100 ÷ 250 = ₹ 0.40 directly.

questions.sourceRef: Purchasing power of the rupee = 100 ÷ cost of living index

questions.stem: Three commodities had base-year prices ₹ 50, ₹ 30 and ₹ 20, and current-year prices ₹ 60, ₹ 39 and ₹ 24. The simple aggregate price index is:

options.explanation: This is the reverse ratio, Σp₀ ÷ Σp₁ × 100 = 100 ÷ 123 × 100. Current prices go on top.
This is the simple average of the three price relatives (120, 130, 120), a different method from the simple aggregate.
This matches only part of the data. Add the three current prices (123) and the three base prices (100) and divide.

questions.topic: Ch 18 · Simple average of price relatives
questions.stem: For four commodities the prices moved 30 → 36, 50 → 65, 20 → 23 and 40 → 44 (base → current). The simple average of price relatives is:

options.explanation: This is the simple aggregate, Σp₁ ÷ Σp₀ × 100 = 168 ÷ 140 × 100. The simple average of relatives averages the four relatives instead.
This is the sum of the four relatives (120 + 130 + 115 + 110) without dividing by N = 4.
Correct. The relatives are 120, 130, 115 and 110, and their average is 475 ÷ 4 = 118.75.
This does not match the average of the four relatives. Sum 120 + 130 + 115 + 110 = 475 and divide by 4.

readLink.label: Read: Simple average of price relatives, §4 →

questions.sourceRef: Simple average of relatives = Σ(p₁ ÷ p₀ × 100) ÷ N

questions.stem: A commodity cost ₹ 150 in the base year and ₹ 180 in the current year. Its price relative is:

options.explanation: This is the reverse ratio, 150 ÷ 180 × 100. The current price divided by the base price gives the relative.
This is the rupee change ₹ 30, not a relative. A relative is a ratio expressed as a percentage.
This is the percentage rise, (180 − 150) ÷ 150 × 100. The relative is the whole ratio, 120.
Correct. Price relative = 180 ÷ 150 × 100 = 120, a 20% rise over the base year.

questions.stem: Three commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (6, 10, 10, 12); B (2, 20, 3, 25); C (4, 15, 5, 10). The Marshall-Edgeworth price index is:

options.explanation: Correct. Marshall-Edgeworth = (Σp₁q₀ + Σp₁q₁) ÷ (Σp₀q₀ + Σp₀q₁) × 100 = (235 + 245) ÷ (160 + 162) × 100 = 480 ÷ 322 × 100 = 149.07.
This is the Laspeyres index, Σp₁q₀ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Marshall-Edgeworth uses (q₀ + q₁) as the weight.
This is the Paasche index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₁ × 100. Marshall-Edgeworth combines both weights.
This is the value index, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Marshall-Edgeworth adds the base and current quantity weights instead.

questions.stem: Four commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (5, 50, 8, 60); B (8, 40, 10, 30); C (12, 20, 15, 25); D (4, 100, 5, 90). The Dorbish-Bowley price index is:

options.explanation: This is the Laspeyres index alone. Dorbish-Bowley is the arithmetic mean of Laspeyres and Paasche.
This is the Paasche index alone. Dorbish-Bowley averages Laspeyres and Paasche.
This is the sum of Laspeyres and Paasche without dividing by 2. Dorbish-Bowley is their mean.

questions.stem: Four commodities have (p₀, q₀, p₁, q₁): A (5, 50, 8, 60); B (8, 40, 10, 30); C (12, 20, 15, 25); D (4, 100, 5, 90). The Fisher quantity index is:

options.explanation: This is the Laspeyres quantity index, Σp₀q₁ ÷ Σp₀q₀ × 100. Fisher is the geometric mean of the Laspeyres and Paasche quantity indices.
This is the Fisher price index. The quantity index weights quantities by prices, not prices by quantities.
Correct. Laspeyres quantity = 1200 ÷ 1210 × 100 = 99.17 and Paasche quantity = 1605 ÷ 1600 × 100 = 100.31, so Fisher quantity = square root of (99.17 × 100.31) = 99.74.
This is the Paasche quantity index alone, Σp₁q₁ ÷ Σp₁q₀ × 100. Fisher takes the geometric mean of it and the Laspeyres quantity index.

readLink.label: Read: Quantity and value index numbers, §11 →

questions.sourceRef: Fisher quantity index = square root of (Laspeyres quantity × Paasche quantity)

questions.topic: Ch 18 · Cost of living · Family budget
questions.stem: A consumer price index has four groups with (group index R, weight W): Food (160, 40); Clothing (120, 20); House rent (130, 25); Fuel (110, 15). By the family budget method the index is:

options.explanation: This is Σ(RW) before dividing by ΣW. The weights total 100, so divide 13,700 by 100.
This is the unweighted mean of the four group indices, (160 + 120 + 130 + 110) ÷ 4. The family budget method weights each index by W.
An index of 100 would mean no change. The weighted total gives 137.

questions.sourceRef: Cost of living (family budget) = Σ(RW) ÷ ΣW

questions.topic: Ch 18 · Fixed base vs chain base
questions.stem: In a fixed-base index series, each year's index is computed with reference to:

options.text: One fixed base year, the same for every year in the series
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed-base series compares every year with a single chosen base year, whereas a chain-base series compares each year with the immediately preceding year.

options.text: The immediately preceding year
options.explanation: That describes a chain-base (link relative) series. In a fixed-base series the reference year does not move.

options.text: The average of all the years in the series
options.explanation: The base is a single chosen year set at 100, not an average of all years.

options.text: The year with the lowest prices
options.explanation: The base is chosen as a normal year, not the cheapest. It need not have the lowest prices.

readLink.label: Read: What an index number is, §1 →

questions.sourceRef: Fixed base compares every year with one base year

questions.stem: Index numbers are often described as economic barometers because they:

options.text: Fix the prices of commodities in the market
options.explanation: Index numbers measure price change; they do not set prices. A barometer registers pressure, it does not create it.

options.text: Measure the net change in the general level of prices or activity, signalling the state of the economy
options.explanation: Correct. Like a barometer registering pressure, an index number registers the net movement of many prices or quantities and so signals inflation, cost of living and output trends.

options.text: Guarantee that wages will always rise faster than prices
options.explanation: Index numbers inform wage revision but guarantee nothing about the outcome. They measure, they do not promise.

options.text: Replace the need for any statistical averaging
options.explanation: An index number is itself a form of weighted average; it uses averaging rather than removing the need for it.

readLink.label: Read: What an index number is, §1 →
